title: Upasiva's question (Sn 5)
hookLine: read it: what can I rely on to cross?
tomorrow: in the middle of a flood, is there anywhere to stand?

lines: CLUTCHING THE EDGE OF THE POOL.
cards: A first swim lesson. The kid clutches the edge of the pool, then the teacher's arm, then a foam board, anything solid. The next student on the way to the far shore, Upasiva, asks for exactly that.
Alone, he says, with nothing to lean on, I can't cross this great flood. Give me a support, something to rely on. And the Buddha's answer is the odd detail.
The support he offers is nothingness. Why would anyone hand a drowning man nothing?

teach.b: In Upasiva's question the Buddha says: mindful, looking to nothingness, relying on the thought there is nothing, cross the flood. Let go of sense pleasures, give up doubting talk, and watch craving end, night and day.
Here's the solve. Upasiva asked for a support, and the word, arammana, also means an object the mind rests on, the way a meditator rests on the breath.

So the Buddha gives him one: a place for the mind to rest that isn't another thing to clutch. Every other support, a person, a plan, a possession, can be grabbed, and whatever you grab is one more thing to drag across.
Nothingness can't be grabbed. Leaning on it, you let go. The swimmer's last lesson is the same: you float when you stop clutching.
Then Upasiva pushes. What happens to the one who gets there?

teach.h: A REST THAT CAN'T BE CLUTCHED.
teach.b: The answer is a picture worth keeping: like a flame blown out by the wind, it goes to rest and can't be counted; so the sage, freed from name and body, goes to rest and can't be counted.
And when Upasiva asks whether that means he doesn't exist, the Buddha says there's no measure for such a one; every way of speaking about him has fallen away.

teach.h: NO MEASURE FOR SUCH A ONE.
teach.b: So what I rely on, in this poem, is not a thing at all.

how: In Theravada meditation, the base of nothingness is a deep, formless absorption; Upasiva's question is also read for its image of the freed sage as a flame gone out, beyond reckoning.

o: a monk's question about where to sleep in the rain
a question about which raft is strongest for a river
a student's plea for a support to cross the flood alone

p: a support to cross the flood
goes to rest, can't be counted
there's no measure for such a one

s: the Buddha tells Upasiva to rely on nothing, meaning give up and stop caring
he gives him a practice: mindful, looking to nothingness, letting go of craving night and day.
in this poem, the freed sage is compared to a flame blown out by the wind
it goes to rest and can't be counted; so the sage, freed from name and body.
the Buddha says plainly that the freed sage simply stops existing
asked that directly, he says there's no measure for such a one; every way of speaking has fallen away.

games.q: a friend just lost her job and asks what she can lean on now that the plan's gone. what does Upasiva's answer point toward?
o: lean on letting go: rest the mind, loosen the grip, then take the next step.
find the next solid thing fast, another plan, and hold it twice as tight.
lean on nothing, meaning stop caring what happens to her at all.
games.why: Upasiva asked for something to hold. the Buddha gave him a rest that can't be clutched: mindful, looking to nothingness, letting craving end.

practice: Let the chair or the floor hold you completely, as if you'd just stopped carrying yourself. Notice where it takes your weight: the back, the seat, the feet.
Then, for the rest of the sit, let even the noticing go, and rest on nothing in particular, only the breath coming and going on its own.

wordCard.voice: Upasiva's question: alone and unable to cross, a student asks for a support. The Buddha points him to nothingness, a rest that can't be clutched, and to the flame that goes out.

orig.note: Pali: support, the object the mind rests on. What Upasiva asks for.

carryVoice: A line to lean on: what I rely on is less, not more. Day sixteen seventy-five, afloat.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 5.7 (Upasivamanavapuccha, Upasiva's question, in the Parayanavagga)
